clue.text: Worker was returning no hawk to Hamlet

parts.note: a hand is a manual worker, as in farmhand

indicators.note: returning means the word for 'was' is read backwards here

parts.note: saw, as in 'I saw', stands in for the verb was

explanation.surface: A labourer coming back to the prince of Denmark without a bird of prey.
explanation.walkthrough: Hamlet says he knows 'a hawk from a handsaw' when the wind is southerly, so to him this tool is certainly no hawk. 'returning' turns WAS into SAW.
explanation.definitionFit: Hamlet's line contrasts the bird with a carpenter's cutting tool, the thing that is not a hawk to him.

clue.text: Ham's mixed with bacon — driver overlooked it

indicators.note: mixed means the letters of the two words are combined and scrambled together

explanation.surface: Cooking instructions combining ham and bacon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mixed' shuffles HAMS and BACON. In this two-wheeled horse carriage the driver sat high up behind, looking down over it.
explanation.definitionFit: The Victorian carriage whose cabman perched above and behind the passengers.

clue.text: Damages Lord's ?--That's black-hearted

indicators.note: a black heart means the letter for black sits in the middle of the word

parts.note: nobles are peers, members of the House of Lords; the question mark admits the stretch
B is the standard abbreviation for black, as on pencils

explanation.surface: Harm at Lord's cricket ground called a wicked act.
explanation.walkthrough: Lord's is a London cricket ground, which colours the surface; 'black-hearted' puts B inside NOBLES. To nobble is to tamper with, as a racehorse is nobbled.
explanation.definitionFit: To nobble is to sabotage or tamper with, as a doped horse is.

clue.text: Shelve half of record, and a bit more

parts.note: a gramophone record has two sides, so one side is half of it
a track is a smaller part of a record, one song

explanation.surface: Putting away part of a vinyl album and then a little more.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shelve' looks like storing records; it means postponing a plan.
explanation.definitionFit: To divert attention from an issue is to put it aside.

clue.text: If divided we fall — Adam's did

indicators.note: we is split apart by the word if placed in its middle

explanation.surface: The motto 'divided we fall', applied to Adam's household.
explanation.walkthrough: 'divided' puts IF inside WE; 'fall' does double duty in the sense: Adam's spouse Eve did fall, tempted by the serpent.
explanation.definitionFit: Eve, Adam's spouse, fell first, so the clue describes her role.

clue.text: " Of Mice and Men " was written shortly after these

definitions.text: " Of Mice and Men " was written shortly after these

parts.words: " Of Mice and Men " was written shortly after these
parts.note: Burns wrote that the best-laid plans of mice and men often go astray; in his Scots the phrase is shortened, and Steinbeck took his title from it

explanation.surface: A literary history note on when Steinbeck wrote his novella.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Written shortly after' does not mean later in time: in Burns's poem 'To a Mouse' the words 'o' mice an' men' come immediately after this word in the line.
explanation.definitionFit: Plans or plots, the Burns word that precedes 'o' mice an' men'.

clue.text: One way and another, I'll stop

definitions.text: One way and another, I'll stop

parts.words: One way and another, I'll stop
parts.note: both 'stand' and 'still' can mean halt, so stopping two ways at once gives a complete halt

explanation.surface: Someone vowing to quit by some means or other.
explanation.walkthrough: The two halves each mean stop, one way and another, and together they mean a dead halt.
explanation.definitionFit: A complete halt, with no movement at all.

clue.text: In place of St Augustine, a beast

definitions.meaning: St Augustine was bishop of a North African city, and is named after it
a large river animal of Africa, short for its Greek name

explanation.surface: An animal standing in for a saint.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In place of' suggests substitution; it means the place Augustine came from.
explanation.definitionFit: Augustine's see in Roman Africa, and the African river-horse, shortened.

clue.text: Not the army one was regularly in ?

definitions.text: Not the army one was regularly in ?

parts.words: Not the army one was regularly in ?
parts.note: a citizen force of part-time soldiers is not the regular army, so a man who served in it was not a regular

explanation.surface: Asking whether someone was a regular soldier.
explanation.walkthrough: 'regularly' plays on regular soldiers: a reserve force of civilians is not the regular army.
explanation.definitionFit: A body of civilian soldiers, distinct from professional forces.

clue.text: Brief her to take legal action

definitions.text: Brief her to take legal action

parts.words: Brief her to take legal action
parts.note: a woman's name whose short form sounds like the verb for going to law against someone

explanation.surface: Instructing a lawyer to sue on a woman's behalf.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brief' looks like briefing a lawyer; it means shortened, and the shortened name is the word for taking legal action.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman's name, commonly shortened to Sue.

clue.text: Statement by West, say, leaving a lot to be desired ?

definitions.meaning: in bridge West is one of the four players, and passing in the auction is said with these words

definitions.text: leaving a lot to be desired
definitions.meaning: an auction lot that nobody offers money for is left unsold, still wanted by its owner

explanation.surface: A remark by some film star called West that is a disappointment.
explanation.walkthrough: West suggests Mae West, but it is a bridge seat; 'a lot' is not 'much' but an item in a sale.
explanation.definitionFit: A call of pass in a bridge auction, and the outcome when an item at a sale draws no offers.

clue.text: Jack up one of these

parts.note: a jack is a small national flag flown at sea, the Union Jack being the famous one, and it is hoisted on a tall pole

explanation.surface: Instructions to raise a car with a jack.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jack up' reads as raising a car; here Jack is the Union Jack flag, run up on a mast.
explanation.definitionFit: Tall staffs from which banners are flown.

clue.text: Young Bunters in lowest form?

definitions.note: Billy Bunter, the fat schoolboy of Frank Richards's Greyfriars stories, was nicknamed the Owl of the Remove

indicators.note: form is read as a verb, the letters of lowest are formed into a new word

explanation.surface: Junior Bunter-like pupils placed in the bottom class at school.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in lowest form' looks like the bottom class at a British school; 'form' is the anagram signal working on LOWEST. Billy Bunter, a comic schoolboy, wore big spectacles and was called the Owl.
explanation.definitionFit: Bunter was 'the Owl', so his young are baby owls.

clue.text: Gilpin's Canadian goal ?

parts.note: in Cowper's comic poem John Gilpin's runaway horse carries him past his destination, a district of north London that shares its name with the capital of Alberta

explanation.surface: Asking where a man called Gilpin was heading in Canada.
explanation.walkthrough: John Gilpin, in William Cowper's ballad, rode for the Bell at a north London village and was carried far beyond it; the question mark admits the Canadian city is only a namesake.
explanation.definitionFit: Gilpin's destination in the poem is a London district whose name the capital of Alberta also bears.

clue.text: Scan a new layout round river for boats

indicators.note: round means the rearranged letters are placed around the river
a new layout is a rearrangement, so the letters of 'Scan a' are reordered

parts.note: the Tamar is the river between Devon and Cornwall

explanation.surface: Redesigning a page around a river picture for a boating magazine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'new layout' turns SCAN A into CAANS, which goes 'round' TAMAR, a river dividing two English counties.
explanation.definitionFit: Twin-hulled sailing vessels are a kind of boat.

clue.text: One taking Cassius' part more than Caesar's

definitions.text: One taking Cassius' part more than Caesar's

parts.words: One taking Cassius' part more than Caesar's
parts.note: in Shakespeare's Julius Caesar this conspirator sides with Cassius against Caesar and strikes the first blow

explanation.surface: An actor who prefers playing Cassius to playing Caesar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Taking a part' suggests acting; it means siding with Cassius. As a bonus, the name starts with CAS from Cassius followed by CA from Caesar, more of the first than the second.
explanation.definitionFit: The conspirator in Julius Caesar who backs Cassius and stabs Caesar first.

clue.text: Sign showing how US motor industry is going ?

definitions.text: Sign showing how US motor industry is going ?

parts.words: Sign showing how US motor industry is going ?
parts.note: auto is the American word for a car, and a chart plotting sales would show the state of carmaking; read as one word it is a signature

explanation.surface: An economic indicator of Detroit's fortunes.
explanation.walkthrough: The chart picture splits the word into car plus diagram; 'Sign' is the true definition, a signature.
explanation.definitionFit: A person's handwritten signature, as collected from celebrities.

clue.text: Soldier makes defensive move on board

definitions.text: Soldier makes defensive move on board

parts.words: Soldier makes defensive move on board
parts.note: on a chessboard a piece is a man, and one guarding another makes a defensive move; read as one word it is a household-troops soldier

explanation.surface: A soldier taking cover aboard ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on board' suggests a ship; it is a game board, where a man guards. The Guards are elite British regiments.
explanation.definitionFit: A soldier of one of the Guards regiments.

clue.text: End of bay where the sailor is wrecked ?

indicators.note: a wrecked sailor's letters are broken up and reassembled

explanation.surface: A sailor shipwrecked at the far end of a bay.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is wrecked' shuffles THE SAILOR. 'bay' looks like a coastline but is a reddish-brown horse, whose rear end is this.
explanation.definitionFit: A bay is a horse, and the hairy appendage at its rear is its end.

clue.text: Oppose introduction of jet missile

parts.note: jet is a deep glossy colour, so jet-black
a ball is something thrown, a missile in a game

explanation.surface: Objecting to the launch of a jet-propelled rocket.
explanation.walkthrough: 'jet missile' sounds like a weapon; it is a colour and a thrown object. In a club, voting with a black ball keeps a candidate out.
explanation.definitionFit: In club elections a black ball in the ballot box vetoes a new member's admission.

clue.text: Dreadful to see so many engulfed in a minute

indicators.note: engulfed in means the pieces are swallowed inside the other phrase

parts.note: wee means tiny, minute
taken as written
M is the Roman numeral for a thousand, a great many

explanation.surface: A grim sight: so many swallowed up in sixty seconds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'minute' is not sixty seconds but tiny, WEE. 'engulfed in' puts SO and M inside A WEE.
explanation.definitionFit: Inspiring dread, the older sense of awe-inspiring.

clue.text: Half of wine comes from an elder tree

indicators.note: comes from means these letters are taken out of the phrase an elder
half of a four-letter word is two letters, here the back pair of wine

explanation.surface: Elderberry wine said to be made from an elder tree.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Half of wine' gives NE; 'comes from' removes those letters, N then E, from AN ELDER, leaving A L D E R.
explanation.definitionFit: A birch-family tree of damp ground.

clue.text: Collect information to get rid of a barrister ?

parts.words: Collect information to get rid of a barrister ?
parts.note: a brief is slang for a barrister, and the prefix de- means removal

explanation.surface: Gathering facts in order to sack one's lawyer.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as de- plus brief, it means dismissing a barrister, a brief in slang; the real sense is questioning someone after a mission.
explanation.definitionFit: To question someone after a mission to gather information.

clue.text: Shetland's odd writer

indicators.note: odd means peculiar, so the letters of Shetland are disordered into another name

parts.note: the 's only shows possession or stands for 'is', so it adds no letters: the word before it gives these letters as it is written

explanation.surface: A strange author from the Shetland Isles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'odd' rearranges SHETLAND; the possessive 's gives no letter.
explanation.definitionFit: The French novelist of The Red and the Black, a pen name of Henri Beyle.

clue.text: A fur that's practical if non- U

indicators.note: non- means without, so the letter is removed

parts.note: something usable is practical, fit for use
U is upper-class, as in Nancy Mitford's U and non-U

explanation.surface: A fur coat that is useful only for the less posh.
explanation.walkthrough: Non-U, Nancy Mitford's term for not upper-class, here means removing U from USABLE.
explanation.definitionFit: The dark pelt of a small Asian marten-like animal is a fur.

clue.text: Trick using, for example, odd anagram

indicators.note: anagram tells the solver to rearrange the letters of odd plus the abbreviation

parts.note: e.g. is short for exempli gratia, for example

explanation.surface: Cheating by using a strange anagram, for instance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'anagram' shuffles ODD and EG; 'odd' looks like the indicator but is fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A clever ruse or ploy is a trick.

clue.text: Unbelievable ending may be swallowed

indicators.note: only the ending is wanted, so the front of the synonym is dropped

parts.note: incredible means unbelievable

explanation.surface: An incredible conclusion that people might accept as true.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ending' keeps the end of INCREDIBLE, losing INCR. 'Swallowed' plays on believing a story.
explanation.definitionFit: Food fit to eat can be safely gulped down.

clue.text: State of Connecticut, a heavenly part

indicators.note: part means only a stretch of the following words is taken

explanation.surface: Connecticut is described as a slice of heaven.
explanation.walkthrough: 'part' marks the run of letters across 'Connecticut, a heavenly'; 'State' tempts as Connecticut itself.
explanation.definitionFit: A US state, home of Salt Lake City.

clue.text: Performance of low-grade US actresses ?

parts.note: broad is American slang for a woman, and a company of performers is a cast, so a cast of broads; the whole word means a radio or television transmission

explanation.surface: A review of a show by second-rate American actresses.
explanation.walkthrough: Split, it is a cast of broads, US slang for women; whole, it is a programme sent out on air.
explanation.definitionFit: A transmitted radio or television programme is a performance sent out to listeners.

clue.text: Man affected by Turner, the artist — girl, too

parts.note: an affected man refers to himself with the French word for me, as Miss Piggy does
J M W Turner was a Royal Academician, RA

explanation.surface: Someone influenced by the painter Turner, and a young woman as well.
explanation.walkthrough: 'by' just places the pieces side by side. RA, Royal Academician, is the usual crossword artist, and Turner was one.
explanation.definitionFit: A female given name, of Irish origin.

clue.text: Scrutinize court decisions for loopholes

parts.note: to eye something is to look at it closely
on a tennis court a let is the umpire's call to replay a point

explanation.surface: Lawyers examining legal rulings for ways round them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'court decisions' and 'loopholes' suggest law; the court is a tennis court and the holes are small rimmed ones for laces.
explanation.definitionFit: Small reinforced holes for laces or cord are holes for loops to pass through.

clue.text: Duke's content, some say, to be troublesome type

definitions.meaning: dukes is slang for fists, so what a duke holds is as much as a fist can grip, as people put it
a person hard to control, such as an unruly child

explanation.surface: A duke's fortune being a source of trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Duke' is a nobleman on the surface; in slang 'dukes' are hands, as in 'put up your dukes'.
explanation.definitionFit: A small amount held in one hand, and a person who is difficult to manage.
